summary: Specifies forty-two cipher suites that let TLS use the Camellia block cipher. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines forty-two ways for TLS to use the Camellia encryption algorithm. Each option combines Camellia with a key-exchange method and other security choices.

subtitle: Forty-two TLS cipher suites let connections use the Camellia block cipher.

tldr.problem: TLS needed suite definitions for using Camellia with several key exchanges, authentication choices, and encryption modes.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines forty-two suites combining Camellia with CBC or GCM, SHA-2 authentication, and several key-exchange methods.
tldr.outcome: It adds Camellia choices to TLS. The unit metadata says RFC 8996 and RFC 10015 update this document.

today: RFC 6367 is informational. The unit metadata lists RFC 8996 and RFC 10015 as updates to it.

sections.title: Camellia Choices for TLS
sections.content:
TLS uses a cipher suite to identify the cryptographic choices for a connection. Earlier work had already defined some Camellia suites; this RFC adds suites using SHA-2, Galois/Counter Mode (GCM), elliptic-curve methods, and pre-shared keys.

The document defines forty-two suites. It builds on existing TLS rules for the key exchanges and describes how each suite combines those rules with Camellia.
sections.plainLanguage: A cipher suite is a named set of security methods for a TLS connection. This RFC adds forty-two such sets that use Camellia.

sections.title: The Cipher Suite Groups
sections.content:
The RFC groups the suites by how they authenticate and encrypt data. The HMAC group uses Camellia in Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode with a SHA-2 hash-based message authentication code. The GCM group uses authenticated encryption with Camellia.

A third group uses pre-shared keys (PSKs), which are secret keys already shared by the parties. Across these groups, the suites specify different key-exchange methods and Camellia key sizes.
sections.plainLanguage: The suite names describe combinations of encryption, authentication, and key exchange. Some use CBC with HMAC; others use GCM, and some use a key the parties already share.

sections.title: Keys, Modes, and Hash Functions
sections.content:
Camellia CBC suites use either a 128-bit or 256-bit key and a 128-bit initialization vector. The GCM suites follow the corresponding AES-GCM definitions, using the same key sizes and block length described by the RFC.

For TLS 1.2, suite names ending in SHA256 use HMAC-SHA-256, while those ending in SHA384 use HMAC-SHA-384. The RFC specifies use of the TLS version's own pseudorandom-function rules for earlier TLS versions.
sections.plainLanguage: The suite name indicates whether Camellia uses a 128-bit or 256-bit key and which SHA-2 hash is used. CBC also uses a 128-bit initialization value; GCM provides authenticated encryption.

sections.title: Security and Registration
sections.content:
The authors report that, at the time of writing, they knew of no weak Camellia keys and had found no security problems with Camellia. They also state that relevant security considerations from the cited TLS and authenticated-encryption specifications apply.

The RFC records the suite identifiers assigned by IANA. It is an informational document, not a Standards Track specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors reported no known Camellia weakness when they wrote this RFC, and point readers to related security rules. The memo is informational and records the identifiers for its suites.
